newsitem.title: PERU: Peruvian rebels rule out "executing" hostages.
newsitem.headline: Peruvian rebels rule out "executing" hostages.

text.p: Marxist rebels in Lima pledged on Wednesday they would not "execute" any of their 74 hostages but warned that the deadlock in negotiations was pushing the crisis towards a violent end.

"It is not in our minds to carry out executions, nor to give any ultimatums," a rebel spokesman, who identified himself as Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini, said in a radio conversation with foreign news media monitored by Reuters.
"We have never spoken of executions," he added.

But Cerpa also said that without tangible progress in negotiations, the crisis was "being pushed towards a military end" where the government would take responsibility for any injury to hostages in a possible storming of the residence.
"The government proposes a peaceful solution but at the same time says it does not have anything to negotiate with us," Cerpa added.
In a step towards possible negotiations, Cerpa said the group has accepted in principle the idea of a "guarantor" commission proposed by the government to oversee talks.
"In what the government is proposing, they are talking about holding (negotiations) in a suitable atmosphere. We will try to do this as far as the circumstances permit," Cerpa said.
But the rebel leader also warned the government that his comrades would not accept a peaceful end to the crisis that involved their surrender.

"The peaceful way out is not where we go out laying down our arms and giving up. That is impossible," he said. Cerpa also denied the guerrillas were demanding ransom money for the Japanese businessmen among the hostages.
The MRTA wants Guatemala and a European country to sit on the negotiating commission in addition to the Red Cross and the Vatican as proposed by the Peruvian government.
Guatemala's ambassador to Peru, Jose Maria Argueta, himself a former captive, has said he would return to the residence to help in the crisis if the Peruvian government approved.
Cerpa insisted the commission should supervise talks on their main demand that the government release over 400 jailed comrades. The government has refused to consider this demand.

The guerrillas' statement on the commission was the first move in negotiations since the cancellation on Sunday of a planned face-to-face meeting between Cerpa and government negotiator Education Minister Domingo Palermo. That meeting fell through because the MRTA wanted their main demand to be discussed at the meeting.
The rebels have kept this demand since Dec. 17 when they stormed a lavish reception taking hundreds of hostages.
Cerpa also said the rebels in the residence were handling their captives with "a treatment respectful of their dignity as people." The hostages were all "in a controllable situation," he added.

President Alberto Fujimori was returning to the grim reality of the deadlocked siege on Wednesday after two days of distractions offered by the visit of Ecuador's leader Abdala Bucaram. Fujimori raced around Lima and the provinces with Bucaram on Tuesday, earning support from cheering crowds and praise from the Ecuadorean president for his tough line with the rebels.
"The world supports Peru and its president not backing down on its position because it would set a very bad precedent to negotiate with people who employ chaos and violence," Bucaram said.

Roman Catholic Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani, a close friend of the president named by the Vatican to sit on the proposed guarantor commission, travelled with Fujimori and called on all sides to sit down for talks as soon as possible.

"My constant request is that God move everyone as soon as possible to start a dialogue which surely will bring peace," Cipriani said. "Please, trusting in God, trusting in truth and openness, sit down to talk. We wish for this, and I believe it will soon happen."

Red Cross spokeswoman Cecilia Baux told Reuters the organisation would join the commission if it was formally set up. "We can participate in the commission but only in matters of a humanitarian nature," she said.
